_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. Before you romanize any name, check here. status per entry: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship, give the citation in note), 'provisional' (your romanization, not found in outside sources), 'decided' (a project style call). If you find a better attested form mid-book, change it here AND grep every built chapter for the old form, then rebuild. Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored. Add/rename sections freely (people, organizations, places, terms, ...).

陈养山.cast: The book's subject; a Central Special Branch intelligence officer, born Cheng Yangshan in Shangyu, Zhejiang, 1906.
陈养山.note: Original name 程仰山 Cheng Yangshan; changed to 陈养山 on taking up secret work.

恽代英.cast: CCP youth organizer and editor of China Youth; the man who drew Chen Yangshan to revolution. 1895-1931.

贺龙.cast: Nanchang Uprising commander whom Chen Yangshan shielded in Shanghai in 1927; later a PLA marshal.

章素贞.note: Chen Yangshan's wife; later joined the Central Special Branch.

陈赓.note: Ran the Central Special Branch's operations; recruited Zhang Suzhen.

顾顺章.note: authority.json: agreed 'Gu Shunzhang'. His 1931 defection gutted the CCP underground.

康生.note: Original name Zhang Zongke; also Zhao Rong. Later head of Party intelligence and security; a principal instrument of the Yan’an rectification purges and, in the Cultural Revolution, of mass persecutions.

潘汉年.note: A leading Communist intelligence figure of the 1930s and 1940s; imprisoned in 1955 on a fabricated charge of treason and rehabilitated only after his death.

李克农.note: One of the founders of Communist intelligence; after 1949 a deputy chief of the General Staff and the Party’s senior intelligence official, sometimes called its spymaster.

陈云.note: Later one of the most senior Communist leaders and, after 1978, the chief architect of the Party’s economic policy.

刘鼎.note: Later a founder of the Communist ordnance industry.

刘伯承.note: A famed Red Army and later PLA commander, made one of the ten marshals in 1955.

赵一曼.note: Birth name Li Kuntai, also Li Yichao; a Communist heroine of the resistance in the Northeast, captured and executed by the Japanese in 1936.

田汉.note: The playwright who wrote the words of “The March of the Volunteers,” later the national anthem of the People’s Republic.

兰普逊.note: The book gives the name only as 兰普逊 (Lanpuxun); the man was the (British) head of the Shanghai Municipal Police political branch. “Lampson” is the translator’s reconstruction of the likely Western original and is not certain.

王根英.note: Chen Geng’s first wife, a labor organizer; killed by Japanese troops in 1939 while serving with the Eighth Route Army.

杨献珍.note: Later a well-known Marxist philosopher, persecuted in the 1960s for his thesis that “two combine into one.”

殷鉴.note: So the book prints the name; not further identified here beyond his post as secretary of the Shun-Zhi provincial committee.

徐悲鸿.note: China’s most celebrated modern painter, renowned above all for his ink horses.

武和景.note: So the book prints the name (武和景); the man is almost certainly Wu Hujing (武胡景), who took over the Special Branch’s work after the Party center left Shanghai. Rendered here as printed.

杨登瀛.note: The cover name Bao Junfu used inside the Kuomintang secret service.

王庸.note: Chen Geng’s cover name in the Central Special Branch.

贺芝华.note: He Jiaxing's wife (also called Hao Zhihua), his fellow informer against Luo Yinong.

郝芝华.note: An alternate name for He Yihua, He Jiaxing's wife.

谭余保.note: First head of the Red Terror Squad; later a guerrilla leader in the Hunan-Jiangxi border area.

颜昌颐.note: A member of the Central Military Commission, executed with Peng Pai at Longhua in 1929.

邢士贞.note: A member of the Jiangsu Provincial Military Commission, executed with Peng Pai at Longhua in 1929.

张际春.note: Deputy chief of the Shanghai General Labor Union pickets, arrested with the Peng Pai group in 1929.

叶挺.note: A leading Communist commander of the Nanchang and Guangzhou uprisings; later commander of the New Fourth Army.

白云深.note: Bai Xin's younger brother, an official in the Nanjing Ministry of Military Administration; Bai Xin's channel to the Kuomintang.

范争波.note: A Kuomintang Shanghai municipal Party figure and secret-service man who sheltered Bai Xin.

范争洛.note: Fan Zhengbo's brother, killed in the Red Squad attack on Bai Xin.

王容川.note: A man who came to see Bai Xin off; wounded in the attack.

韩云秀.note: Fan Zhengbo's bodyguard, shot in the attack on Bai Xin.

林汉臣.note: A gatekeeping patrolman at Fan Zhengbo's residence.

王宝元.note: A gatekeeping patrolman at Fan Zhengbo's residence.

范梦菊.note: Owner of the Sanmin Photo Studio; he brought the weapons late to the failed rescue of the Peng Pai group, and later turned traitor.

柯达文.note: Ke Lin's cover name as a doctor at the Dasheng Hospital.

贺诚.note: A Communist doctor, co-founder of the Dasheng Hospital cover clinic; later a founder of the army medical service and a deputy health minister.

邵达夫.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

谭忠余.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

王德明.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

赵一帆.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

吴蓝甫.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

陈永嘉.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

左光余.note: A Red Squad member in the Bai Xin operation.

王松生.note: A Shanghai hooligan who peddled political intelligence; a link in the Chen Weinian case.

玉香.note: Huang Dihong's young cousin at his aunt's home in Shanghai.

陈昌.note: A veteran Communist underground worker, one of the Three Chens in Chongqing; see the footnote at his first appearance.

贾绍谊.note: An alternate name for Chen Chang.

刘其珍.note: Chen Chang's wife, sent with him to open the Chongqing intelligence front in 1935.

陈克寒.note: A Communist journalist, one of the Three Chens; later a senior figure at the Xinhua News Agency and a deputy minister of culture.

陈仲英.note: Chen Yangshan's cover name in Chongqing.

刘航琛.note: Financier of Liu Xiang's Sichuan regime, from whom the Communists took over the New Sichuan News Agency.

刘湘.note: The dominant Sichuan warlord of the 1930s, based at Chongqing.

康泽.note: A Blue Shirts leader and head of the Kuomintang's Special-Operations Corps; captured by Communist forces in 1948.

袁福禄.note: Secretary to Kang Ze; the connection through which the Three Chens entered the Special-Operations Corps.

王世英.note: A veteran Communist intelligence officer who headed the Central Special Branch in its final phase (1935).

邱吉夫.note: A Shanghai liaison man for Chen Yangshan, arrested in November 1935.

冯雪峰.note: A writer and literary theorist, a Long March veteran sent to Shanghai in 1936 to rebuild Party contacts and liaise with Lu Xun.

陶敬之.note: A progressive journalist on the Chongqing press cultivated by the Three Chens.

温嗣翔.note: Romanization provisional (scan reading of the given name uncertain); a progressive journalist on the Chongqing press.

侯珍昌.note: A progressive journalist on the Chongqing press cultivated by the Three Chens.

黄应乾.note: Secretary of the Chongqing municipal government, a Zhongtong man.

李鸿混.note: Romanization provisional (the character hun is doubtful in the scan); a Chongqing mayor of Liu Xiang's faction.

袁家佩.note: Commander of the Third Gendarmerie Regiment at Chongqing.

李介民.note: Head of the Chongqing field headquarters' press-censorship office; a Communist defector.

孙中山.note: The founder of the Kuomintang and of the Whampoa Military Academy; conventional English form retained.

宋绮云.note: Source prints 宗绮云 (Zong) at first mention; 宋绮云 (Song) is the attested form.

塞先佛.note: Crop-verified 塞 (base 土); an uncommon surname.

陈鸣钧.note: Chen Yangshan's cover name at the Xi'an station.

丘金.note: A Yan'an cadre; not the martyr 秋瑾 of the same romanization.

震宇.note: Chen Yangshan's younger son, Chen Zhenyu.

冈野进.note: The Yan'an alias of Nosaka Sanzo, of the Japanese Communist Party.

陈建宇.note: Chen Yangshan's eldest son, called Jianyu.

王明.note: Chen Shaoyu; leader of the returned-students faction.

武胡景.note: Also known as Wu Huairang (武怀让).

苏枚.note: A sister of Kang Sheng's wife Cao Yi'ou.

基洛夫.note: Sergei Kirov, the Leningrad Party leader assassinated in 1934.

李文芳.note: Cover name of Zhang Xinfu (张新甫), the 'Xinfu' of Chen Yangshan's letter.

崔守安.note: Formerly Wang Lianzhong (王连仲); the 'Lianzhong' of Chen Yangshan's letter.

张和.note: Intelligence officer who penetrated the enemy service in Guisui; took the name 张又新 Zhang Youxin after Liberation.

张达志.note: Cavalry-brigade commander, later a PLA lieutenant-general.

薛英.note: Zhang He's wife, who worked with him under cover in Guisui.

冀述楷.note: Guisui intelligence-station head; not to be confused with Wang Shukai.

魏岗.note: A man of Hengshan in northern Shaanxi; Kuomintang figure turned CCP connection, later commanded the 4th Suiyuan Security Regiment; his regiment defected in 1949.

方少明.note: A cover name of 王雁鸣 Wang Yanming.

王雁鸣.note: Datong intelligence organizer; also used the names Fang Shaoming, Wang Bozhong, and Wang Huaibao.

高克林.note: Secretary of the CCP Saibei district committee and head of its Social Affairs Department; later a senior PRC judicial official.

楚溪春.note: Yan Xishan general who later took part in the peaceful handover of Beiping.

中原.note: Japanese major-general, deputy director of the Yanbei office of the Resource Investigation Society; given name not recorded.

韩步洲.note: Commander of Yan Xishan's 38th Division at Datong.

鲁南.note: Codename of the Suiyuan intelligence agent 赵锡鸿 Zhao Xihong, also called 赵孚民 Zhao Fumin; the codename echoes his Shandong origin (Lu = Shandong).

赵孚民.note: An alternate name of Lu Nan (Zhao Xihong).

李启明.note: Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region Security Office officer who ran and later vetted Lu Nan; not to be confused with Li Fushan.

何绍南.note: Kuomintang commissioner and security commander at Suide, driven out by CCP forces in 1940.

陈奇涵.note: PLA general, later president of the PLA Military Court.

马占山.note: Anti-Japanese general famous for resisting the Japanese in Manchuria in 1931.

陈长捷.note: Nationalist general, later the defeated defender of Tianjin in 1949.

李禾亭.note: Inspection-station chief at Dongsheng and a Juntong agent.

贾耿夫.note: Juntong agent who arrested Lu Nan and Gong Zhen at Dongsheng.

马汉三.note: Juntong chief in Suiyuan and head of the Eighth War Zone anti-smuggling office; the source also spells his name 马汉山 Ma Hanshan.

马汉山.note: The source's alternate spelling for Ma Hansan (see 马汉三).

欧阳钦.note: Senior CCP official of the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region Security Office; later a provincial Party leader.

张庆恩.note: Chief of the Suiyuan Investigation and Statistics secret service and KMT provincial party secretary-general; fled to Taiwan in 1949.

曲日新.note: Intelligence worker whose memoir the chapter draws on.

刘珍.note: Teacher at Huangzhai who bought enemy books and papers for the intelligence network.

周佛海.note: A founding Communist turned Kuomintang figure, then a leading collaborator in Wang Jingwei's puppet government.

陈公博.note: A founding Communist turned Kuomintang figure, later head of Wang Jingwei's puppet regime; executed in 1946.

周高明.note: Courier; the source gives his name as both 周高明 Zhou Gaoming and 田高明 Tian Gaoming.

田高明.note: The source's alternate surname for the courier Zhou Gaoming.

李芳.note: Jin-Sui Military Region reconnaissance staff officer who led the raid to seize Nanqi.

南奇.note: Chinese name of the Japanese officer Nakamura Rijin, a quartermaster at Lanxian seized in a 1944 raid.

中村里仁.note: Japanese officer also known by the Chinese name Nanqi.

郑贵.note: Datong-born agent who cracked the Bureau of Confidential Investigation's Suiyuan network.

邢绍闻.note: Bureau of Confidential Investigation officer at Guisui, Zheng Gui's sworn brother, turned by him.

何柱国.note: Cavalry general of the Northeastern Army.

庞中兴.note: Head of the Bureau of Confidential Investigation's Suiyuan station until 1949.

毛人凤.note: Head of the Kuomintang's Juntong / Bureau of Confidential Investigation after Dai Li's death.

武毓美.note: Juntong adjutant turned by Zheng Gui, who handed over the Suiyuan Juntong files.

田唆布.note: Bureau of Confidential Investigation North China deputy chief; reading of the name uncertain from the scan.

中央特科.note: authority.json: agreed 'the Central Special Branch' / 'Central Special Branch'. The CCP Central Committee's clandestine intelligence and security organ, Shanghai, from 1927.

工部局.note: The Shanghai Municipal Council, governing body of the International Settlement.

红队.note: The Central Special Branch’s armed unit, the Third Section, which guarded the Party’s organs and carried out the assassination of traitors and enemy agents. Its nickname among the underground was the “dog-beating squad.”

党务调查科.note: Full title the Investigation Section of the Kuomintang Central Organization Department, set up in 1928 under Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu; the forerunner of the “CC Clique” secret service that became the Central Statistics Bureau (Zhongtong).

中统.note: Zhongtong, the Kuomintang party’s civilian intelligence and secret-police organ, as distinct from the military Juntong.

淞沪警备司令部.note: The Kuomintang military garrison authority for the Shanghai–Wusong area, with wide powers of arrest and execution over the Chinese-administered districts.

巡捕房.note: The police of the foreign concessions; in the International Settlement the Shanghai Municipal Police, in the French quarter the French concession police. A xunbufang was a patrol house or station.

青帮.note: The largest of Shanghai’s secret-society brotherhoods, deep in the city’s labor, opium, and protection rackets and closely tied to the Kuomintang after 1927.

同盟会.note: The Revolutionary Alliance, Sun Yat-sen’s pre-1912 revolutionary organization and the forerunner of the Kuomintang; a member of it was a founding revolutionary of the Republic.

申报.note: Shanghai’s oldest and most widely read Chinese newspaper.

大公报.note: A leading independent Chinese daily, then published in Tianjin.

莫斯科东方大学.en: the Communist University of the Toilers of the East
莫斯科东方大学.note: The Moscow academy (KUTV) that trained Asian Communists in the 1920s.

顺直省委.note: The Party committee for the Hebei region around Beiping and Tianjin; “Shun-Zhi” is the old provincial name Zhili.

《中国青年》.note: The Socialist Youth League's magazine, edited by Yun Daiying.

红色恐怖队.note: The formal name given the Red Squad on its 1928 reorganization under the Central Special Branch.

武德学会.note: A body Liu Xiang formed to bind his Sichuan followers together against Chiang Kai-shek's faction.

别动队.note: Kang Ze's Kuomintang paramilitary and intelligence corps.

新四川通讯社.note: The Chongqing news agency the Three Chens took over as intelligence cover, 1935-37.

南华通讯社.note: A Shanghai-and-Wuhan news agency the Special Branch ran as intelligence cover.

复兴社.note: The Blue Shirts, a militant Nationalist body tied to the military-intelligence Juntong.

重庆行辕.note: The Nationalist military field headquarters at Chongqing.

政训处.note: The political-training (and intelligence) organ of the Military Affairs Commission; its Chongqing branch funded the Three Chens' agency.

中央社.note: The Kuomintang's official wire service, founded in 1924.

民国日报.note: The Kuomintang's newspaper; the Shanghai edition ran from 1916.

上海日报.note: A Shanghai newspaper Bao Junfu carried folded as a recognition signal.

新蜀报.note: A progressive Chongqing newspaper (Shu being the classical name for Sichuan).

达生医院.note: A clinic on Weihaiwei Road run by Communist doctors as cover for the Party's Shanghai apparatus.

上海临时中央局.note: The Party's provisional leading organ in Shanghai in the mid-1930s, after the main leadership moved to the soviet areas.

红中通讯社.note: Forerunner of the New China (Xinhua) News Agency.

三青团.en: the Three People's Principles Youth Corps

同志会.note: Yan Xishan's political mass organization, the 'Comradeship Association for the Sacrifice to Save the Nation'.

保密局.note: The Nationalists' Bureau of Confidential Investigation (Baomiju), the postwar successor to the Juntong (Bureau of Investigation and Statistics).

调统室.note: A provincial organ of the Kuomintang's party investigation-and-statistics (intelligence) system; rendered 'Investigation and Statistics' throughout.

特种会议秘书处.note: A Suiyuan secret-service body fronting the Investigation and Statistics system.

资源调查社.note: A Japanese secret-service organ later taken over by Yan Xishan.

晋绥情报总局.note: Chen Yangshan's intelligence organization in Jin-Sui, also called the Investigation Bureau and the Public Security General Bureau as it was renamed.

牺盟会.note: The Shanxi Sacrifice for National Salvation League, a united-front body under Yan Xishan that the CCP heavily influenced.

中华民族解放先锋队.note: A CCP-led patriotic youth organization founded in 1936.

协和医院.en: the Peking Union Medical College Hospital
协和医院.note: Beijing’s foremost modern hospital, founded by the Rockefeller Foundation.

北平.note: The name Beijing bore from 1928, when the Nationalists moved the capital to Nanjing, until 1949; literally “northern peace.”

鄂豫皖苏区.note: One of the largest Communist base areas of the early 1930s, in the border hills where the three provinces meet.

毕勋路.note: A leafy street of the French Concession, today Fenyang Road.

静安寺路.note: A main thoroughfare of the International Settlement, today part of West Nanjing Road.

海陆丰.note: Haifeng and Lufeng counties of eastern Guangdong; site of Peng Pai's 1927 peasant soviet.

霞飞路.note: A main avenue of the Shanghai French Concession, today Huaihai Middle Road.

城隍庙.note: A temple and bazaar district in the old walled city of Shanghai.

先施公司.note: A pioneering Nanjing Road department store, opened in 1917.

绥远.note: A former province in present-day Inner Mongolia; scene of a 1936 anti-Japanese campaign.

万县.note: A Yangtze river city in eastern Sichuan (now Wanzhou), where Chen Chang was moved in 1937.

扬州.note: A city in Jiangsu on the Grand Canal.

闸北.note: A district of Shanghai north of Suzhou Creek.

平凉路.note: A road in the eastern part of the International Settlement.

赫德路.note: A road in the western International Settlement, now Changde Road.

卡德路.note: A road in the International Settlement, now Shimen No. 2 Road.

威海卫路.note: A Shanghai road, now Weihai Road.

小沙渡路.note: A road in western Shanghai, now Xikang Road.

湖北路.note: A road in the central International Settlement.

西安.note: The capital of Shaanxi; Chen Yangshan was transferred there in 1936.

浦东.note: The east bank of the Huangpu River at Shanghai.

归绥.note: Former name of Hohhot (now capital of Inner Mongolia); called Houhehaote under Japanese occupation.

大同.note: Major coal city in northern Shanxi.

集宁.note: City in Suiyuan (now Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia).

伊克昭盟.note: Mongol banner-league in the Ordos region, south of the Yellow River bend (now Ordos).

河套.note: The great bend of the Yellow River in western Suiyuan.

杀虎口.note: A pass on the Shanxi-Suiyuan border (its name means 'Kill-Tiger Pass').

陕坝.note: Wartime seat of the Suiyuan provincial government, in the Hetao.

长征.note: The Communist forces' 1934-35 fighting retreat from the southern soviets to a new base in northern Shaanxi.

全国苏维埃代表会议.note: The May 1930 Shanghai gathering of soviet-area delegates that prepared for a national soviet government.

抗日救亡运动.note: The mass movement for resistance to Japan that rose in the mid-1930s.

卢沟桥事变.note: The Marco Polo Bridge Incident, 7 July 1937.

辽沈战役.note: The decisive September-November 1948 campaign in the Northeast.

绥远和平起义.note: The September 19, 1949 defection of Suiyuan under Dong Qiwu, on the 'Suiyuan formula.'

苦肉计.note: A classic stratagem: injuring oneself or sacrificing one's own to make a feigned defection credible.
